Neonates of the Sharptooth houndshark emerge at a total length of approximately 31 cm [Lb = approximately 31 cm], a size that reflects the substantial yolk investment characteristic of triakid sharks. This length at birth has been documented in field captures of near-term gravid females along the southern African coastline, where the species is most commonly encountered. The gestation period, inferred from closely related species such as Mustelus antarcticus, proceeds at a water temperature of 19.3 °C [T = 19.3 °C] and yields an age at birth of roughly 350 days [ab = roughly 350 days]. This prolonged developmental phase is consistent with the slow life-history strategy typical of many demersal elasmobranchs, where extended embryogenesis within the mother is thought to enhance the size and presumed survival of pups at parturition. Newborn individuals are immediately capable of independent foraging, having absorbed their internal yolk reserves completely prior to birth, and they quickly disperse into shallow, nursery-like habitats where prey availability is high.

As female Sharptooth houndsharks progress through their juvenile phase, they undergo a gradual increase in body length that culminates in the attainment of sexual maturation. The total length at puberty for females has been measured at 58.3 cm [Lp = 58.3 cm], a value derived from dissections that revealed the onset of ovarian activity and the presence of developing follicles. At this life stage, the corresponding wet weight at puberty is approximately 840 grams [Wwp = approximately 840 grams], indicating that females invest considerable somatic resources into growth before the initiation of reproductive function. This length and mass represent a clear inflection point in the species' ontogeny, marking the transition from an immature organism focused on mass gain to a reproductively viable adult capable of supporting the energetic demands of gestation. The onset of gonadal maturation is accompanied by changes in body condition and feeding ecology, as mature females begin to allocate more resources toward the production of yolk and the maintenance of developing embryos during repeated breeding cycles.

The ultimate total length attained by adult Sharptooth houndsharks has been recorded at 92 cm [Li = 92 cm], representing the asymptotic size approached by the oldest and largest individuals in wild populations. This maximum recorded body length is consistent with observations from long-term mark-recapture studies conducted in the temperate waters of the Agulhas Bank. The wet weight at puberty corresponding to this ultimate length is estimated at 3,500 grams [Wwi = 3,500 grams], a substantial body mass that supports the high energetic costs associated with gestation and the storage of energy reserves needed between reproductive events. Large adult females are capable of carrying multiple litters over their lifetime, though the slow pace of their life history constrains the frequency with which they can reproduce successfully. These measurements highlight the pronounced size dimorphism and capital-breeding strategy that distinguish this species from smaller, more fecund shark species occupying similar benthic habitats.

Reproductive output in the Sharptooth houndshark is characterized by a low fecundity and an extended interval between successive litters. Gravid females typically produce 6 to 12 pups per litter [N_R_i = 6 to 12 pups per litter], a modest litter size that is offset by the relatively large size of individual neonates at birth. The frequency of reproduction is constrained by a biennial cycle, with females producing one litter every two years [F_R_i = one litter every two years], reflecting the prolonged gestation period and the time required to replenish energy stores depleted during pregnancy. These combined parameters yield a maximum reproductive rate of approximately 0.0082 pups per day [Ri = approximately 0.0082 pups per day], which is aligned with the species' K-selected life-history strategy, typical of larger triakid sharks inhabiting productive continental shelf environments. All of these reproductive measurements were recorded under ambient thermal conditions prevailing at 19.3 °C [T = 19.3 °C] in the field, a temperature that represents the average sea surface temperature across much of the species' geographic range.

This longevity, measured at the same ambient temperature of 19.3 °C [T = 19.3 °C], places the species among the longer-lived members of the Triakidae family and is consistent with its slow growth rate and late age at sexual maturity. Individual sharks that survive to this advanced age exhibit signs of reproductive senescence, including reduced fecundity and irregular cycling, before eventually succumbing to physiological death. The combination of a low reproductive rate and a protracted lifespan emphasizes the species' vulnerability to overfishing, as population recovery following exploitation is expected to be slow. Comparative data from related triakid sharks suggest that this lifespan may be near the upper limit for the genus, underscoring the need for careful conservation management given the species' limited demographic resilience.
